sources.title: Programming FAQ: arguments, references and mutable objects (Python docs)
sources.used_for: Arguments are passed by assignment; names refer to objects; y = x does not copy a list; list, dict and set are mutable and str, int and tuple are not; += mutates a list but builds a new int or tuple; default arguments are created once.

sources.title: copy: shallow and deep copy operations (Python docs)
sources.used_for: Assignment never copies; shallow copy inserts references to the same contents; deep copy recursively copies them; deepcopy uses a memo to avoid loops.

sources.title: Data model, section 3.1: objects, values and types (Python docs)
sources.used_for: Every object has an identity, a type and a value; identity never changes and is compared with is; id() is the memory address in CPython; two empty lists are always distinct objects.

sources.title: Divide-and-conquer algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Definition (break into sub-problems, solve, combine); correctness by induction and cost by recurrences; merge sort; binary search as the single-subproblem case; base cases; memoization leads to dynamic programming.

sources.title: Master theorem for divide-and-conquer recurrences (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n); critical exponent log_b a; the three cases; worked results for binary search, tree traversal and merge sort.

sources.title: Design and History FAQ: how are lists implemented in CPython? (Python docs)
sources.used_for: CPython lists are variable-length arrays of references, not linked lists; indexing costs the same for any index; append over-allocates so the next few appends need no resize; sort() sorts in place and returns None.

sources.title: Time complexity of operations on built-in types (Python docs)
sources.used_for: List: append O(1) amortized, insert and delete O(n-k), get and set item O(1), slice O(j-i), x in l O(n), sort O(n log n); string: concatenation is O(len(s)+len(t)), substring search O(n) with a two-way algorithm.

sources.title: Dynamic array (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Growing by a constant factor makes n appends cost O(n) in total, so amortized O(1); insert at the front or middle is Theta(n); CPython list growth factor is about 1.125.

sources.title: Amortized analysis (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Amortized analysis averages operation costs over a sequence; aggregate, accounting and potential methods; dynamic array push is O(1) amortized; two-list queue dequeue is O(1) amortized.

sources.title: Prefix sum (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Cumulative sum y_i = y_(i-1) + x_i; inclusive and exclusive scans; needs only an associative operator; used by counting sort; a Fenwick tree supports updates with logarithmic time.

sources.title: itertools.accumulate (Python docs)
sources.used_for: accumulate(iterable, func, initial=None) yields running totals; the default function is addition; initial adds one extra leading element.

sources.title: Maximum subarray problem (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Kadane's algorithm solves it in O(n) time and O(1) space; the example [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4] has answer 6; all-negative arrays return the largest single element; older O(n^2) and O(n log n) solutions.

sources.title: String-searching algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Naive search O(mn) worst case; Rabin-Karp O(n) average and O(mn) worst; KMP Theta(m) preprocessing and Theta(n) matching; Boyer-Moore and two-way variants.

sources.title: Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: KMP uses a failure table so the text is never re-read; table build is O(k) and search is O(n); naive search can take O(k*n); published 1977.

sources.title: Row- and column-major order (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Row-major stores each row contiguously, column-major each column; C is row-major with offset x + Nx*y; Fortran, MATLAB and Julia are column-major; NumPy defaults to row-major; looping row-wise is preferred in C.

sources.title: Linked list (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A linked list is a linear collection whose order is not given by physical placement in memory; insert or remove is constant time when the node before it is already held; no random access; insert/delete at the beginning is constant, at the end constant only if the end is known; arrays have better cache locality; sentinel nodes give every list a first and last node.

sources.title: Doubly linked list (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Each node has previous and next links; it can be seen as two singly linked lists in opposite orders; head and tail are immediately accessible and traversal runs either way; insertAfter sets new.prev and updates next.prev; removing the first or last node needs special handling; sentinels remove the special cases.

sources.title: Cycle detection (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Floyd's tortoise and hare uses two pointers at different speeds; after they meet, resetting the tortoise to the start and stepping both one at a time finds the cycle start (mu), then the cycle length (lambda); O(lambda + mu) time and O(1) storage; Brent's algorithm is another constant-storage method.

sources.title: Merge sort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Most implementations are stable; O(n log n) worst and average; auxiliary space O(1) with linked lists; the left run is taken on ties for stability; top-down and bottom-up variants; efficient for sequentially accessed data such as linked lists.

sources.title: Cache replacement policies (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: LRU discards the least recently used items first and must track what was used and when; also FIFO, MRU, LFU, random and the pseudo-LRU used by CPUs; LRU is a family including 2Q and LRU/K.

sources.title: Stack (abstract data type) (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Push and pop, LIFO order, peek; underflow on pop or peek of an empty stack and overflow on a full bounded stack; array and linked-list implementations; dynamic-array end operations are amortized O(1); the call stack.

sources.title: Queue (abstract data type) (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front, FIFO; insert and delete O(1); overflow and underflow; circular arrays and linked lists; the two-list amortized queue; uses such as buffering and breadth-first search.

sources.title: Circular buffer (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A fixed-size buffer treated as connected end to end; start and end indexes; start == end cannot tell full from empty, fixed by keeping one slot free or by keeping a count; overwrite or error when full; all queue operations O(1).

sources.title: Double-ended queue (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Insertion and deletion at both ends; input- and output-restricted variants; implemented by a doubly linked list or a modified dynamic array; random access is O(1) in an array deque and O(n) in a linked one; Python's deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-length subarrays.

sources.title: All nearest smaller values (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: The stack algorithm pops while the top is not smaller than the new value; it is linear because each inner-loop pass removes an item pushed earlier; applications include matching parentheses and building a Cartesian tree.

sources.title: Using lists as stacks and queues (Python tutorial)
sources.used_for: append and pop on a list make a stack; inserts and pops at the front of a list are slow; use collections.deque for a queue.

sources.title: collections.deque (Python docs)
sources.used_for: Thread-safe appends and pops from either side with O(1) performance; maxlen discards from the opposite end when full; indexing is O(1) at the ends and O(n) in the middle; rotate, extendleft and the moving average recipe.

sources.title: queue: a synchronized queue class (Python docs)
sources.used_for: Queue, LifoQueue and PriorityQueue; maxsize blocks put when full; get blocks when empty; Full and Empty exceptions; task_done and join; the classes are thread safe.

sources.title: Hash table (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A hash function maps a key to a bucket index; load factor alpha = n/m; chaining versus open addressing; Theta(1) average and O(n) worst case for search, insert and delete; resizing by doubling and rehashing keeps amortized O(1); typical maximum load factors.

sources.title: Open addressing (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Probing finds another slot after a collision; linear, quadratic and double hashing with their clustering and cache trade-offs; load factors normally limited to about 80%; deleting needs a shift-back or a deleted marker.

sources.title: Hash function (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values; it must be deterministic, fast and spread keys uniformly; universal hashing; perfect hashing for a known static set.

sources.title: Bloom filter (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A bit array of m bits and k hash functions; false positives possible, false negatives not; false-positive probability about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k; optimal k = (m/n) ln 2; about 9.6 bits per element for a 1% error; items cannot be removed.

sources.title: Built-in types: dict, set and frozenset (Python docs)
sources.used_for: dict keys must be hashable and dictionaries keep insertion order; get, setdefault, pop, update and views; set is an unordered collection of distinct hashable objects with union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference; frozenset is hashable.

sources.title: Glossary: hashable (Python docs)
sources.used_for: An object is hashable if its hash never changes and it can be compared for equality; equal hashable objects must have equal hashes; lists and dicts are not hashable; a tuple is hashable only if its items are.

sources.title: collections: Counter and defaultdict (Python docs)
sources.used_for: Counter is a dict subclass for counting hashable objects, returns zero for missing items and has most_common; defaultdict calls default_factory for a missing key and is simpler and faster than setdefault for grouping.

sources.title: Binary tree (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Each node has at most two children; full, perfect, complete and balanced trees; height counted in edges; node-count bounds; a complete tree stores in an array with children at 2i+1 and 2i+2; degenerate trees behave like lists.

sources.title: Tree traversal (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Pre-order NLR, in-order LNR, post-order LRN and level-order; in-order on a BST gives ascending keys; stack-based traversal uses O(h) space; pre-order with in-order determines a tree; Morris traversal.

sources.title: Lowest common ancestor (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: The LCA of v and w is the deepest node with both as descendants, and a node counts as its own descendant; root-path method costs O(h); Tarjan's offline algorithm; Euler tour plus range minimum query; dist(v,w) = depth(v) + depth(w) - 2 depth(LCA).

sources.title: Binary search tree (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Ordering property; search, insert and delete are O(h), Theta(log n) average and O(n) worst case; insertion adds a leaf; successor rules; three deletion cases; in-order visits keys in order; degeneration into a list.

sources.title: Self-balancing binary search tree (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Self-balancing trees keep height O(log n) with rotations that preserve in-order sequence; sorted insertion degenerates a plain BST; minimum height floor(log2 n); AVL, red-black, splay and treap examples.

sources.title: AVL tree (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Balance factor in {-1, 0, 1}; the four cases Left-Left, Right-Right, Left-Right and Right-Left fixed by single or double rotations; height below about 1.44 log2 n; search, insert and delete O(log n).

sources.title: Segment tree (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A segment tree answers an associative function over a contiguous range in O(log n); each node covers the union of its children's intervals; stabbing queries O(log n + k); invented by Bentley in 1977.

sources.title: Binary heap (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A complete binary tree with the heap property; insert by sift-up and extract by sift-down, both O(log n); Floyd's build-heap is O(n); array layout with children at 2i+1 and 2i+2; searching is O(n); introduced by Williams in 1964.

sources.title: Heapsort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Build a max-heap in O(n), then repeatedly swap the root to the end and sift down; O(n log n) in all cases, O(1) auxiliary space, not stable; quicksort is usually 2 to 3 times faster in practice.

sources.title: Priority queue (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Insert, find-min, extract-min and decrease-key; unsorted array O(1) insert and O(n) extract, sorted array the reverse, binary heap O(log n) for both; used by Dijkstra, Prim and Huffman coding; Python's heapq is a binary min-heap on a list.

sources.title: Adjacency list (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: One neighbour list per vertex; space proportional to |V| + |E|; listing neighbours costs time proportional to the degree; an edge test is slower than in a matrix; a matrix needs space proportional to |V|^2.

sources.title: Adjacency matrix (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: An n x n matrix with A_ij = 1 for an edge; symmetric for undirected graphs; edge test at once; neighbour listing scans a row, time proportional to |V|; sparse graphs need less space as lists.

sources.title: Breadth-first search (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: BFS explores all nodes at the current depth before the next, using a queue; marks a vertex when it is enqueued; O(|V| + |E|) time; finds shortest paths measured in edges; used to test bipartiteness.

sources.title: Depth-first search (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack; O(|V| + |E|); edges classed as tree, back, forward and cross; reverse postorder gives a topological sort; applications include components and strongly connected components.

sources.title: Component (graph theory) (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A component is a maximal connected subgraph; components partition the vertices; found in linear time with BFS or DFS; union-find handles incremental connectivity in amortized inverse-Ackermann time; a spanning forest has n - c edges.

sources.title: Topological sorting (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A linear order with every edge u -> v placing u first; exists exactly for graphs with no directed cycle; Kahn's algorithm and the DFS-based algorithm, both O(|V| + |E|); unique only when consecutive vertices are joined by an edge; used for build order and task scheduling.

sources.title: Strongly connected component (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Maximal sets of vertices that can all reach each other; contracting them gives a DAG; Kosaraju's two-pass algorithm and Tarjan's one-pass algorithm run in linear time; 2-SAT is unsatisfiable exactly when a variable and its negation share a component.

sources.title: Bellman-Ford algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Relaxes every edge |V| - 1 times; handles negative weights; O(|V||E|); an extra pass that still relaxes an edge reveals a reachable negative cycle; stops early when a round changes nothing.

sources.title: Floyd-Warshall algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: All-pairs shortest paths in Theta(|V|^3) time and Theta(|V|^2) space; recurrence over intermediate vertices k with k as the outer loop; negative edges allowed but no negative cycles; Warshall's transitive-closure variant.

sources.title: Minimum spanning tree (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A spanning tree has n - 1 edges; the minimum one connects all vertices at least total weight; unique when weights are distinct; the cycle and cut properties justify the greedy algorithms of Kruskal, Prim and Boruvka.

sources.title: Prim's algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge to a vertex outside it; O(|V|^2) with an array, O(|E| log |V|) with a binary heap, O(|E| + |V| log |V|) with a Fibonacci heap; works on connected graphs.

sources.title: Kruskal's algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Sort edges by weight and add each edge that joins two different trees, checked with a disjoint-set structure; O(E log E) with the sort dominating; first published by Kruskal in 1956.

sources.title: Binary search (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Binary search needs a sorted array; worst case O(log n) with floor(log2 n + 1) iterations and O(1) space; midpoint L + floor((R - L) / 2); leftmost and rightmost match variants; absent targets give a rank; hash tables are faster for exact lookups.

sources.title: Insertion sort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Worst and average O(n squared), best O(n) on sorted input; stable, in place and adaptive; efficient for small or nearly sorted data and used inside faster sorts below a small threshold; writes O(n squared) versus selection sort's O(n).

sources.title: Selection sort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Repeatedly moves the minimum of the unsorted part to the front; always n(n - 1)/2 comparisons and at most n - 1 swaps; in place; the usual swap version is not stable; useful when writes are costly; heapsort is selection sort with a heap.

sources.title: Bubble sort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs until a pass makes no swap; O(n squared) worst and average, O(n) best with the early exit; stable and in place; rarely used because insertion sort is usually faster.

sources.title: Quicksort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Divide and conquer around a pivot; average O(n log n), worst case O(n squared); in place and not stable; Lomuto and Hoare partition schemes; first or last pivot degrades on sorted input; random or median-of-three pivots help.

sources.title: Quickselect (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Finds the k-th smallest element by partitioning and recursing into one side; average O(n), worst case O(n squared); in place; the shown code assumes Lomuto partitioning; random pivot makes bad cases very unlikely; median of medians gives linear worst case.

sources.title: Counting sort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Counts how many times each integer key occurs, takes prefix sums, then places items stably from the end; O(n + k) time and space; not a comparison sort; practical only when the key range is not much larger than n.

sources.title: Radix sort (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Sorts digit by digit with a stable sort for each digit; least-significant-digit radix sort runs in Theta(d(n + k)); most-significant-digit variants are not necessarily stable; non-comparative.

sources.title: Sorting algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A sort is stable when equal keys keep their input order; comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n) on average; table of common sorts with best, average and worst cases, memory and stability.

sources.title: Greedy algorithm (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders; no formal definition of when it works; exchange arguments; optimal for activity selection, Dijkstra, Kruskal, Prim and Huffman coding; fails on some other problems.

sources.title: Huffman coding (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Builds an optimal prefix code from symbol weights by repeatedly merging the two lowest-weight nodes with a priority queue, in O(n log n); decoding walks the tree bit by bit; optimal among prefix codes for known symbol probabilities.

sources.title: Backtracking (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Builds candidates incrementally and abandons one as soon as it cannot be completed; partial candidates are nodes of a search tree explored depth-first; reject and accept tests; examples include eight queens, Sudoku and SAT solvers.

sources.title: Eight queens puzzle (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: 92 solutions for n = 8, or 12 up to rotation and reflection; solutions exist for every n except 2 and 3; brute force has 4,426,165,368 arrangements, one queen per column cuts it to 8^8 and permutations to 8!; backtracking solves it instantly.

sources.title: Power set (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: The set of all subsets of a set of n elements has 2^n members; subsets correspond to n-bit binary numbers; recursive definition P(S) = P(T) union {t + e for t in P(T)}.

sources.title: Permutation (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: There are n! permutations of n distinct objects; k-permutations number n!/(n-k)!; a derangement has no fixed points.

sources.title: itertools: permutations, combinations and product (Python docs)
sources.used_for: permutations(iterable, r) yields r-length orderings in lexicographic order by position; combinations(iterable, r) yields sorted subsequences; product gives the Cartesian product; counts are n!/(n-r)! and C(n, r).

sources.title: Dynamic programming (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Needs optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; top-down memoization versus bottom-up tabulation; the Fibonacci example turns an exponential recursion into O(n); developed by Bellman in the 1950s.

sources.title: Memoization (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Stores the results of calls to pure functions so repeated calls return the stored value; a space-time trade-off; only valid for referentially transparent functions; normally implemented with a hash table.

sources.title: Knapsack problem (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: 0-1 knapsack maximizes value under a weight limit W; the recurrence m[i, w] runs in O(nW) time, pseudo-polynomial; the decision version is NP-complete; two rows are enough when only the value is needed.

sources.title: Change-making problem (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Minimum number of coins for an amount; dynamic programming in O(nW); greedy works for canonical coin systems but fails for others, for example coins 25, 10, 1 with amount 40 gives 7 coins greedily against 4 optimally.

sources.title: Longest increasing subsequence (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Solvable in O(n log n) time with binary search on smallest tails; the LIS of a sequence equals the LCS of the sequence and its sorted copy; worked example 2, 8, 9, 5, 6, 7, 1 gives 2, 5, 6, 7.

sources.title: Longest common subsequence (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Subsequence elements need not be contiguous; the O(m n) table recurrence on matches and maxima; backtracking from the corner recovers the sequence; ABCD and ACBAD give length 3; used by diff.

sources.title: Edit distance (Wikipedia)
sources.used_for: Levenshtein distance counts insertions, deletions and substitutions; the Wagner-Fischer table takes Theta(m n) time; two rows reduce space to Theta(min(m, n)); kitten to sitting is 3.

levels.label: 0-2 years
levels.title: Entry / junior
levels.focus: Well-defined tasks under guidance. Interviews lean on fundamentals and a coding exercise; design rounds are light or absent.

levels.label: 2-5 years
levels.title: Mid-level
levels.focus: Own features and small projects with more independence. Expect performance tuning, API and schema design, tests by default. In system design you drive requirements, APIs and schemas; breadth matters more than depth.

levels.label: 5+ years
levels.title: Senior
levels.focus: Large features, architectural decisions, mentoring. Fundamentals are assumed; go deep in about two places, flag limits of your own design, discuss failure modes and trade-offs unprompted.

level_note: Band boundaries vary by company. Tech Interview Handbook uses 0-2 / 2-5 / 5+ years; Lemon.io labels Django 'Middle' 3-5 and 'Senior' 5-8 years.
basis_note: Priorities and hour estimates are my own judgment, not a published standard; the sources show where each topic appears in interviews and job posts.
